q: Wednesday evening club race, 8 knots. You and Blue are close-hauled on starboard tack, overlapped, you to leeward, heading straight at a large yacht anchored in the middle of the leg. Which of you decides whether to pass her to port or to starboard?
a: You — the right-of-way boat chooses the side; if you change course to do so you must give Blue room to keep clear
o: Blue — the windward boat chooses because she can see over the obstruction
Blue — whichever boat hails her choice first decides
Neither — both must pass an anchored vessel on the side nearer the next mark
why: Rule 19.2(a): the right-of-way boat may pass an obstruction on either side; if she changes course to do so, she gives the other boat room to keep clear.

fig.note: Both on starboard, Blue to windward

q: You are reaching on port tack, overlapped inside Red — between her and the end of a long concrete pier you both have to pass. Red, outside and to leeward, holds her course and the gap closes. Does Red have to give you room?
a: Yes — once overlapped, the outside boat gives the inside boat room between her and the obstruction, even though Red is the right-of-way boat
o: No — Red is the leeward boat and has right of way, so you must keep clear by slowing down
No — room at an obstruction is owed only to a boat that was clear ahead when it was first reached
Yes, but only if you hailed "Water" before Red reached the pier
why: Rule 19.2(b): when boats are overlapped, the outside boat gives the inside boat room between her and the obstruction, unless unable since the overlap began.

fig.note: Both on port tack, reaching east along the pier

q: Dying breeze, 5 knots, running on starboard. Grey, clear astern of you, surges on a puff and gets an overlap on your inside only a boat length before you both reach a line of moored motor boats. You cannot open a gap in time; she wedges in and touches both a mooring buoy and your quarter. Who broke a rule?
a: Grey — the outside boat need not give room when she has been unable to do so from the time the overlap began
o: You — an outside boat must always give room to an inside overlapped boat at an obstruction
Nobody — a boat astern may squeeze in as long as she gets the overlap before the obstruction
You — as the boat ahead at an obstruction you should have slowed to let Grey through
why: Rule 19.2(b): the outside boat gives room unless she has been unable to do so since the overlap began; Grey must then keep clear (rule 11).

fig.note: Grey has just got the overlap, one length from the moorings

q: 470 nationals, you are beating along a beach on starboard tack, clear astern of 4471. You sail a little lower and faster and become overlapped between her and the shore at a point where there is not enough room for a boat to pass. 4471 does not move over and you have to tack out. Were you entitled to room?
a: No — at a continuing obstruction a boat that gets an inside overlap from clear astern where there is no room is not entitled to it, and must keep clear
o: Yes — once overlapped the outside boat must always give room at an obstruction
Yes — you were the leeward boat, so under rule 11 4471 had to luff and make space
No, but 4471 had to tack away at once as the boat farther from the shore
why: Rule 19.2(c): at a continuing obstruction a boat from clear astern that gets an inside overlap with no room is not entitled to it; rules 10 and 11 are off.

fig.note: You have just got an overlap between 4471 and the beach

q: Saronic Gulf, reaching on starboard along a rocky shore in 12 knots. You come up from clear astern of Red and get an overlap between her and the rocks where there are three lengths of clear water. A minute later the shore juts out, the gap narrows, and Red bears away toward the rocks to close you out. Who is right?
a: You — there was room between Red and the shore when the overlap began, so rule 19.2(b) applies and Red must give you room; 19.2(c) does not bite
o: Red — at a continuing obstruction a boat that comes from clear astern is never entitled to inside room
Red — she may bear away at you as long as she gives you room to keep clear under rule 16.1
Red — a leeward boat cannot claim room against a boat that was ahead of her
why: Rule 19.2(c) denies room only when there was no room between the other boat and the obstruction at the moment the overlap began; otherwise 19.2(b) applies.

fig.note: The shore juts out ahead; Red bears away toward you

q: You and Blue, overlapped on starboard tack, approach the committee boat end of the finishing line. Blue is inside and hails "Room — obstruction!", claiming room under rule 19 to pass between you and the committee boat. Which rule actually governs?
a: Rule 18 — the committee boat is a mark you both must leave on the same side, so Blue is entitled to mark-room, not room under rule 19
o: Rule 19 — a committee boat is a vessel, so it is an obstruction and the inside boat gets room between you and it
Neither — at a finishing mark surrounded by navigable water no room is owed, just as at the start
Rule 19 — because the committee boat is anchored it counts like any other anchored vessel
why: Rule 19.1(a): rule 19 does not apply when the obstruction is a mark the boats must leave on the same side; rule 18 applies at a finishing mark.

fig.note: Finishing at the committee boat end, Blue inside

q: Leeward mark to port, three boats overlapped on starboard: Red inside, Blue in the middle, you outside. Blue is entitled to mark-room from you under rule 18. Blue also hails you for room under rule 19 to pass Red, saying Red is an obstruction to her. Is she right?
a: No — when rule 18 applies between you and the obstruction is another boat overlapped with each of you, rule 19 does not apply; rule 18 alone governs
o: Yes — Red is a boat Blue must keep clear of, so she is an obstruction and rule 19 adds room to the mark-room
Yes — rule 19 always applies at a boat, and rule 18 only at the mark itself
No — a boat racing can never be an obstruction, so rule 19 never involves other boats
why: Rule 19.1(b): rule 19 does not apply when rule 18 applies between the boats and the obstruction is another boat overlapped with each of them.

fig.note: Leave the mark to port; Red inside, you outside

q: Beat in 12 knots. You and Yellow are close-hauled on port, overlapped, you to leeward, Yellow a length to windward. Grey crosses on starboard. You decide to bear away and pass astern of Grey, but Yellow, who also has to duck, is bearing down on you. What must Yellow do?
a: Give you room to pass astern of Grey between her and Grey — Grey is an obstruction to you both and you, the right-of-way boat, chose the side
o: Nothing — Yellow is clear of Grey; if you cannot duck in time you must tack
Tack at once — a windward port-tack boat must always tack when a starboard-tack boat crosses
Hold her course — at an obstruction the boat nearest to it must find her own way round
why: A right-of-way boat is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of her; rule 19.2(a)–(b): you choose the side and Yellow, outside, gives you room.

fig.note: Grey on starboard; both port-tack boats will have to duck her

q: Palma, 36-ft cruiser-racers running on port gybe. You are clear ahead of Blue, who is a length and a half astern on the same tack, and a trawler lies at anchor dead ahead. At the last moment you alter course sharply to starboard; Blue, who was already going that way, has to gybe to miss your stern. Was that allowed?
a: You may choose either side, but when you change course to do it you must give Blue room to keep clear — you did not
o: Yes — a boat clear ahead has no obligation whatever to a boat clear astern
No — you had to pass on the side Blue had committed to, because she chose first
No — you had to hail your choice; without a hail the boat astern picks the side
why: Rule 19.2(a): the right-of-way boat may pass either side, but if she changes course to do so she gives the other boat room to keep clear (as in rule 16.1).

fig.note: You bear away hard to starboard at the last moment

q: You are close-hauled on port tack. Red, close-hauled on starboard, is converging and will cross just ahead of you. Your crew asks: is Red an obstruction to us?
a: Yes — a boat racing is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of her, so Red is one to you, though you are not one to her
o: No — only fixed objects, anchored vessels and the shore are obstructions
Yes, and that means Red must also give you room to pass her
No — a boat is an obstruction only when she is capsized, anchored or aground
why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is an obstruction to other boats only if they must keep clear of her or avoid her under rule 22.

fig.note: Red on starboard, you on port

q: A race committee RIB is holding station on her engine 40 m below the windward mark; the sailing instructions do not list her as a mark. You and Grey, overlapped and close-hauled on starboard, must pass her; Grey is inside, between you and the RIB. What are Grey's rights?
a: Grey is entitled to room to pass between you and the RIB under rule 19 — the RIB is an obstruction, not a mark
o: None — the RIB is a mark boat, so rule 18 applies and Grey gets mark-room only if overlapped at the zone
None — a vessel with her engine running is never an obstruction to boats racing
None — Grey is the windward boat and must keep clear of you whatever is in her way
why: Definition Obstruction and rule 19.2(b): a vessel you cannot pass without a substantial course change is an obstruction; the outside boat gives room.

fig.note: Grey inside, between you and the RIB

q: Lake regatta. The sailing instructions declare the swimming area, marked by yellow buoys, a prohibited area. You and Blue are overlapped on starboard, reaching along its edge, you inside. Blue says no room is owed because "a few buoys are not an obstruction". Who is right?
a: You — an area that a rule prohibits boats from entering is an obstruction by definition, so Blue, outside, must give you room
o: Blue — only a solid object you could hit can be an obstruction under the rules
Blue — the prohibited area binds each boat separately and creates no rights between boats
You, but only because the buoys themselves are marks of the course
why: Definition Obstruction (c): an object, area or line so designated by a rule that boats may not enter or cross; rule 19.2(b) then applies.

fig.note: Reaching west along the prohibited area, you inside

q: You are overlapped inside Red, to windward, passing the head of a pier on port tack. Red, the leeward boat, luffs you toward the pilings and you touch a piling and then her hull; no damage. Who is penalised?
a: Red — she had to give you room; you are exonerated for breaking rule 11 and for the contact, as you were sailing within the room you were entitled to
o: You — a windward boat must keep clear whatever the obstruction; the pier is your problem
Both — Red for luffing and you for the contact, because rule 14 applies to every boat
Nobody — luffing is allowed and touching a pier is not a breach of any racing rule
why: Rule 19.2(b) binds the outside boat; rule 43.1(b)–(c): the inside boat sailing within her room is exonerated for breaking rules 11 and 14 (no damage).

fig.note: Red luffs you toward the pier head

q: Lake race in 6 knots. A tall navigation post stands in the middle of the second leg; it is not a mark of the course. You and Black are overlapped on starboard, you inside and nearer the post. Black says you cannot claim room "because it isn't a mark". Is she right?
a: No — the post is an obstruction and, being overlapped, Black as the outside boat must give you room to pass between her and it
o: Yes — room is owed only at marks of the course and at other boats
Yes — a post with navigable water all round can be passed either side, so no room is owed
No, but only if you were clear ahead when the post was two lengths away
why: Definition Obstruction (an object a boat could not pass without a substantial course change) and rule 19.2(b); a post needs no status as a mark.

fig.note: You inside, nearer the post

q: Bodrum, 15 knots. Blue, inside and to windward of you, is given room to pass between you and an anchored gulet. She swings out much wider than she needs, well clear of the gulet, and her boom hits your shrouds. She says she was "within her room". Was she?
a: No — room is the space needed to pass in a seamanlike way; sailing wider than that she was no longer within it and broke rule 11 as windward boat
o: Yes — an inside boat may use all the space the outside boat gives up until both are past the obstruction
Yes — rule 19 gives the inside boat right of way until both boats are clear of the obstruction
No, but you are penalised too, for not giving extra room in the waves
why: Definition Room: space to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; rule 43.1(b) exonerates only a boat sailing within that room.

fig.note: Blue swings wide of the gulet and into you

q: Run in 10 knots. You are on starboard tack, Blue on port, both sailing more than 90° from the wind and side by side, approaching an anchored ship. Blue is nearer the ship. Must you give her room to pass between you and the ship?
a: Yes — boats on opposite tacks are overlapped when both sail more than 90° from the wind, so rule 19.2(b) applies and you, outside, give room
o: No — rule 10 gives you right of way and a port-tack boat is never entitled to room from a starboard-tack boat
No — boats on opposite tacks cannot be overlapped, so rule 19.2(b) cannot apply
Yes, but only once Blue has gybed onto starboard tack
why: Definition Overlap: opposite-tack boats are overlapped when both sail more than 90° from the true wind; rule 19.2(b) then applies between them.

fig.note: Both running; Blue inside, nearer the ship

q: Thirty seconds to the start. Blue, overlapped to windward of you, squeezes between you and the committee boat and hails "Room — obstruction!". Must you give her room?
a: No — the committee boat is a starting mark in navigable water: rule 18 is off while approaching to start and rule 19 does not apply at a mark; rule 11 governs
o: Yes — the committee boat is a vessel, so it is an obstruction and the inside boat is entitled to room under rule 19 until she is past it
Yes — a boat overlapped inside when the pair reaches the zone of the committee boat is entitled to mark-room under rule 18.2(a)
No — before the starting signal no boat has a proper course, and therefore no boat can be entitled to room of any kind
why: Rules 18.1 and 19.1(a): no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water and no rule 19 room at a mark; the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11).

fig.note: 30 s before the start; Blue barging at the committee boat

q: Just after the start, you and Red are close-hauled on starboard, overlapped, heading between the committee boat and the small buoy marking her anchor 25 m upwind of her. You are inside, nearer the anchor line. Red says the anchor line is part of the mark and no room is owed. What is the anchor line?
a: An obstruction, not part of the mark — overlapped boats passing it are subject to rule 19, so Red must give you room
o: Part of the mark — touching it is a rule 31 breach and rule 18 applies to it
Nothing — only the hull of the committee boat has any status under the rules
A mark — anything attached to a mark boat, including her ground tackle, is part of her
why: Rules 18.1 and 19.1(a): no mark-room at a starting mark in navigable water and no rule 19 room at a mark; the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11).

fig.note: You inside, heading between the committee boat and her anchor buoy

q: Reaching leg, you are the windward boat overlapped with Red, who is to leeward. A spectator boat is anchored on the course ahead. Red bears away to pass to leeward of her. Must you pass on the same side as Red?
a: No — Red, the right-of-way boat, chooses her side and you must keep clear of her; if you can pass the other side while keeping clear, you may
o: Yes — overlapped boats must pass an obstruction on the same side, the side chosen by the right-of-way boat
Yes — the windward boat always follows the leeward boat's side at an obstruction
No — as the windward boat you choose your side first and Red adjusts to it
why: Rule 19.2(a) gives the right-of-way boat the choice of side; the other boat's duty is to keep clear (rule 11), on whichever side she can do so.

fig.note: Red bears away to pass to leeward of the spectator boat

q: The fleet beats up a narrow river. To port is a quay with forty yachts moored along it; ahead a small fishing boat lies at anchor. Which of them is a continuing obstruction?
a: The line of moored yachts along the quay — the small anchored fishing boat is an ordinary obstruction
o: Both — any object you cannot pass without a substantial course change is a continuing obstruction
The fishing boat — a vessel at anchor is always a continuing obstruction
Neither — only natural shoreline counts as a continuing obstruction
why: A continuing obstruction is one boats sail alongside for some time (a shore, a long quay, a line of moored boats); a short object is an ordinary obstruction.

fig.note: A small fishing boat is anchored further up the river

q: River race with two knots of current under you. You and Blue are overlapped on port, reaching toward the bridge arch the sailing instructions tell you to use; you are inside, nearer the pier of the bridge. How much room must Blue give you?
a: Room to pass between her and the pier in a seamanlike way in the existing conditions — which here includes space for the set of the current
o: Exactly one hull length between you and the pier; the current is your own problem
None — a bridge pier is not an obstruction because the arch is a designated passage
Only room to keep clear of Blue herself; the pier is not her concern
why: Rule 19.2(b) and definition Room: the space needed in the existing conditions to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way — current included.

fig.note: Current sets you toward the upper pier

q: You are close-hauled on port, Red close-hauled on starboard; your courses converge right at an anchored barge. Red hails that she is the inside boat and demands room between you and the barge. Does she get it?
a: No room is owed — on a beat opposite-tack boats are not overlapped, so rule 19.2(b) cannot apply; rule 10 governs and you keep clear of Red
o: Yes — Red, as right-of-way boat, is entitled to room between you and the barge under rule 19.2(b)
No — you are the inside boat and are entitled to room, so Red must bear away
No — both boats must pass the barge on the side nearer the next mark, and neither owes room
why: Definition Overlap: boats on opposite tacks on a beat are not overlapped; rule 19.2(b) needs an overlap, so only rule 10 applies.

fig.note: Courses converge at the barge

q: Beating along a sea wall on starboard tack. Blue came from clear astern and wedged in between you and the wall where there was no room; you had to pinch to avoid contact. Now the wall falls away and there is plenty of water. Still overlapped, Blue hails "Leeward boat — up, up!" May she now claim rights under rule 11?
a: No — for as long as that overlap lasts she must keep clear and rules 10 and 11 do not apply; the gap opening later gives her nothing
o: Yes — as soon as there is room between you and the wall the normal rules return and she is the leeward boat
Yes — rule 19.2(c) only applies at the moment the overlap begins, not afterwards
No — but you must now give her room under rule 19.2(b) because room has become available
why: Rule 19.2(c): a boat that got the inside overlap without room is not entitled to it and, while the overlap lasts, keeps clear; rules 10 and 11 do not apply.

fig.note: Blue got the overlap earlier where there was no room

q: The course passes through a 40 m gap in a breakwater. Three boats arrive overlapped on starboard: White nearest the gap wall, you in the middle, Grey outside. Who owes room to whom?
a: Grey must give you room, and you must give White room — each outside boat gives the boat inside her room to pass between her and the obstruction
o: Grey gives room to White only; the middle boat has no rights and no duties under rule 19
You give room to White, but Grey owes you nothing because you are not nearest the wall
Nobody — a gap in a breakwater is a passage, not an obstruction, so rule 19 is off
why: Rule 19.2(b) applies between each pair of overlapped boats: the outer gives the middle room, and the middle, as outside boat to the inner, gives her room too.

fig.note: The gap is between the two walls; White nearest the left wall

q: Split, a Mediterranean regatta. A rock awash is marked on the chart but has no buoy. You and Red are overlapped on port, reaching, you inside and nearer the rock. Red says that without a buoy it is "not an obstruction under the rules". Who is right?
a: You — an object a boat one length away heading at it could not pass without a substantial course change is an obstruction, buoyed or not; Red gives you room
o: Red — only objects marked on the water or listed in the sailing instructions are obstructions
Red — a rock is part of the seabed, and the rules deal only with objects on the surface
You, but only because the chart counts as part of the sailing instructions
why: Definition Obstruction (a): an object a boat could not pass without substantially changing course if she were one hull length from it; rule 19.2(b) applies.

fig.note: You inside, nearer the rock

q: You are close-hauled on port tack, three lengths from a stone quay, with Blue close to windward of you so that you cannot tack without hitting her. You hail "Room to tack!". Is your hail allowed?
a: Yes — you are close-hauled, approaching an obstruction, and will soon need a substantial course change to avoid it safely
o: No — you may hail only when you are already within one hull length of the obstruction
No — a leeward boat may not hail; room to tack is for the windward boat
Yes, but only if you first hailed "Water" and waited for a reply
why: Rule 20.1: a boat may hail for room to tack when approaching an obstruction, about to need a substantial course change, and sailing close-hauled or above.

fig.note: You will hit the quay in three lengths unless you tack

q: You are on a reach, about 20° below close-hauled, with the shore coming up and Blue just to windward. You hail "Room to tack!"; Blue tacks at once and then protests you. What should the protest committee decide?
a: You are penalised: you hailed while not sailing close-hauled, breaking rule 20.1; Blue was right to respond, as she must even to an improper hail
o: Blue is penalised: a boat that responds to a hail accepts it and cannot protest afterwards
Nobody: on a reach the hail is simply void and Blue could have ignored it
Both are penalised: you for hailing and Blue for responding to an invalid hail
why: Rule 20.1(b): hail only when sailing close-hauled or above; rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat responds even if the hail breaks rule 20.1.

fig.note: You are reaching, well below close-hauled

q: Beating up a shoreline, Red, close to leeward of you on the same tack, hails "Room to tack!". Which responses satisfy the rule?
a: Tack as soon as possible, or reply "You tack" at once and then give Red room to tack and to avoid you
o: Reply "Hold your course" and bear away to give her room to tack beneath you
Tack as soon as possible, or ignore the hail if you can see she could still bear away
Reply "You tack" and keep your course; Red must then tack and keep clear of you
why: Rule 20.2(c): the hailed boat either tacks as soon as possible or immediately replies "You tack" and gives the hailing boat room to tack and avoid her.

fig.note: Red to leeward hails for room to tack

q: You hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack at a pier. She replies "You tack!" but then holds her course and you have to abort your tack to avoid her stern, ending up pinching along the pier. Who broke a rule?
a: Blue — after replying "You tack" she had to give you room to tack and to avoid her
o: You — once Blue replied you had to tack and keep clear of her under rule 13 whatever room there was
Nobody — "You tack" transfers the whole responsibility to the hailing boat
You — you should have tacked before hailing instead of waiting for Blue's answer
why: Rule 20.2(c): a hailed boat that replies "You tack" must then give the hailing boat room to tack and to avoid her.

fig.note: Blue replied "You tack" but did not move over

q: A 20° header hits you on the beat, far from any shore or boat you must avoid. Grey is sitting on your windward quarter, so you cannot tack without fouling her. You hail "Room to tack!" to get across onto the lifted tack. Is that allowed?
a: No — the hail is allowed only when approaching an obstruction; Grey must still respond, but she may protest you
o: Yes — a boat may hail for room to tack whenever another boat prevents her from tacking
Yes — a header of 20° or more is a reason that justifies requiring room to tack
No, and Grey may simply ignore the hail because there is no obstruction
why: Rule 20.1: a hail is permitted only when approaching an obstruction; rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat responds even if the hail breaks rule 20.1.

fig.note: The wind has headed you 20°; no obstruction anywhere

q: Windward mark to be left to port. You and Red are both close-hauled on starboard in the zone, Red to windward and fetching the mark, you a little below the layline and heading straight at the mark. You hail Red "Room to tack!" to avoid hitting the mark; she tacks away and you round. What happened under the rules?
a: You broke rule 20.1 — no hail for room to tack when the obstruction is a mark and a boat fetching it would have to change course; Red nevertheless had to respond
o: Nothing wrong — the mark is an obstruction and you were close-hauled, so the hail met every condition of rule 20.1
Red broke rule 20.2 — a boat fetching a mark may refuse to respond to a hail for room to tack, and she should have
Both acted correctly — Red's tack counted as giving you mark-room under rule 18.2(a)
why: Rule 20.1, last sentence: no hail when the obstruction is a mark and a boat fetching it would have to change course; rule 20.2(b): she still responds.

fig.note: Red is fetching the mark; you are heading straight at it

q: Three boats close-hauled on port toward a sea wall: Yellow to leeward, you in the middle, Black to windward. Yellow hails you "Room to tack!". You cannot tack because Black is right beside you to windward. What do you do?
a: Hail Black for room to tack at once, then tack as soon as she responds — between you and Black rule 20.2 applies
o: Reply "You tack" to Yellow — a boat that cannot tack is excused from responding
Bear away under Yellow's stern; the hail does not bind a boat that has another boat to windward
Wait until Black tacks of her own accord; you may not hail unless you are the leeward boat
why: Rule 20.3: a hailed boat that intends to tack may hail another boat on the same tack for room to tack, even if her own hail would not meet rule 20.1.

fig.note: Yellow has hailed you; Black is close to windward of you

q: Approaching a shoal marked by a pole, you hail "Room to tack!" and put the helm down in the same breath. Red, to windward, has no time to react and your bow hits her quarter. Who broke a rule?
a: You — after hailing you must give the hailed boat time to respond before you tack; until she responds you have no right to tack into her
o: Red — once hailed she had to tack instantly, and she did not
Nobody — the collision was caused by the shoal, which is nobody's fault
Red — a windward boat must anticipate a hail whenever an obstruction is near
why: Rule 20.2(a): after hailing, a boat gives the hailed boat time to respond; tacking at once she also breaks rule 13 while past head to wind.

fig.note: You hailed and tacked at the same moment

q: Blue tacked immediately when you hailed her for room to tack at a rocky point. Now, with Blue gone, you look again and think you can just squeeze past the point without tacking. May you hold on?
a: No — once the hailed boat has responded, you must tack as soon as possible
o: Yes — the hail only obliges the hailed boat; the hailer may then do as she pleases
Yes — if the obstruction can be cleared after all, the hail is cancelled automatically
No — you had to tack before Blue did; the hailing boat always tacks first
why: Rule 20.2(d): when the hailed boat responds, the hailing boat shall tack as soon as possible.

fig.note: Blue has already tacked in response to your hail

q: Beat along a lee shore off Split in 25 knots and breaking waves. You need room to tack and hail Red at the top of your voice, but her crew, hiking hard, clearly hear nothing. What does the rule require of you?
a: You must also make a signal that clearly indicates your need for room to tack — in such conditions the hail alone is not enough
o: Nothing more — a loud hail satisfies the rule whether or not it is heard
You must call Red on VHF channel 16; no other method is recognised
You cannot ask for room; in heavy weather rule 20 is suspended for safety
why: Rule 20.4(a): when conditions mean a hail may not be heard, the boat must also make a signal that clearly indicates her need for room to tack (or her response).

lines: Wind 25 knots, breaking waves
You: close-hauled on port, 3 lengths off the shore
Red: close to windward, same tack
You hail "Room to tack" — no reaction

q: You hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack at a harbour wall. Blue replies "You tack!", but Red is close to windward of Blue and Blue cannot move over; you are forced to bear away along the wall. Who broke a rule?
a: Blue — having replied "You tack" she had to give you room; she should have tacked, or passed the hail on to Red and then tacked
o: Red — the outermost boat is always responsible for making room when a hail is made
You — you should have hailed Red directly, as the boat that was actually in the way
Nobody — Blue did all she could; rule 20 does not apply when three boats are involved
why: Rule 20.2(c): after "You tack" the hailed boat must give room; rule 20.3 lets her instead hail a third boat and tack when that boat responds.

fig.note: Blue replied "You tack" but Red pins her

q: You are close-hauled on port, a few lengths from the shore. Grey, close-hauled on starboard, is crossing just ahead of you. You hail Grey "Room to tack!". What is the effect?
a: None — rule 20 works only between boats on the same tack; Grey keeps her rights under rule 10 and you must keep clear of her
o: Grey must respond by tacking or replying "You tack" — the hail binds any boat within hearing
Grey must respond, because an obstruction cancels rule 10 between boats near it
Grey may ignore the hail, but she must still give you room under rule 19
why: Rule 20.1: a boat may hail for room to tack and avoid a boat on the same tack; across tacks rule 10 applies and the hail has no effect.

fig.note: Grey is on starboard, you on port

q: The windward mark, to be left to port, is laid three lengths off a rocky point. You and Blue are close-hauled on port in the zone, Blue to windward and inside for the rounding; the rocks are dead ahead. You hail Blue "Room to tack!" and she tacks; you tack after her. Blue later protests that you failed to give her mark-room. Decision?
